scenario.name: Microsoft Print Spooler, Kaspersky & MITRE DFIR — Print Spooler Port Monitor & .SPL/.SHD Spool Forensics (EID 307 / 808)
scenario.overview: Imagine a high-ceiling logistics warehouse with towering steel pallet racks stacked with labeled shipping crates, clipboard dock stations, and a bright yellow forklift cruising down the aisle. Inside the bustling logistics warehouse, an unverified driver climbs into a parked yellow forklift and rolls toward the high-bay customer storage racks. In this real-world scenario, the intruder approaches the loading dock check-out clipboards disguised as a regular visitor, then bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the high-bay pallet racks & forklift. The warehouse barcode inventory system flashes an urgent alert when hundreds of customer pallets are relabeled in minutes outside normal shift hours. In this scenario (T1547.012, Microsoft Print Spooler, Kaspersky & MITRE DFIR, Print Spooler Port Monitor & .SPL/.SHD Spool Forensics , EID 307 / 808), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: mS-RPRN / MS-PAR RPC Bind to \\pipe\\spoolss, then port Monitor Registration via AddMonitor, then sYSTEM DLL Load in spoolsv.exe. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering MS-RPRN / MS-PAR RPC Bind to \\pipe\\spoolss, then Port Monitor Registration via AddMonitor, then SYSTEM DLL Load in spoolsv.exe, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 11 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 2: Port Monitor Registration via AddMonitor & PrintService EventID 316 / 808
stages.subtitle: Privilege Escalation (T1547.012 - Print Port Monitor Registry & EventID 808)
stages.description: Lifting stacked pallets off the shelves, the driver slaps a brand-new shipping barcode and their own heavy padlock onto every customer crate in the bay. Here in Step 2 inside the logistics warehouse, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the logistics warehouse later without disturbing the quarantined audit cage. The attacker invokes winspool.drv!AddMonitorW (or RpcAddMonitor) to register evilmon.dll as a Print Port Monitor. This creates HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver="evilmon.dll" (Sysmon EventID 13) and logs Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational EventID 316 (Printer driver added) and EventID 808 (Failed/Untrusted plug-in module load in spoolsv.exe) (logged in WinEvent Event 808 with LogChannel=Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational, EventID=808 , Spooler Plug-in Load / 316 , Driver Added, RegistryPersistenceKey=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver, LoadedModule=C:\Windows\System32\evilmon.dll so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes AddMonitorW(NULL, 2, &monitorInfo2) -> Registers Driver="evilmon.dll" (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , AddMonitorW, NULL, 2, &monitorInfo2 -> Registers Driver="evilmon.dll" via evilmon.dll, passi so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1547.012 during "Port Monitor Registration via AddMonitor & PrintService EventID 316 / 808" , The attacker invokes winspool while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact Registry Key: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver runs (which Modifies or queries Windows Registry keys and values , Registry Key: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver via th so that extracts the 16-byte SysKey / BootKey , stored across the JD, Skew1, GBG, and Data registry classes under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa required to decrypt the PEK and password hashes inside ntds.dit or SAM , T1547.012). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ spoolsv.exe loading C:\Windows\System32\evilmon.dll via Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor / ⇠#2 ACK 808) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 MS-RPRN \pipe\spoolss RPC), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Print\Monitors & spool\PRINTERS).

stages.title: Stage 3: SYSTEM DLL Load in spoolsv.exe (Sysmon EventID 7) & Child Shell Execution (Sysmon EventID 1)
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1547.012 - spoolsv.exe ImageLoad & SYSTEM Child Process)
stages.description: When the real warehouse dispatcher arrives for morning pickup, every pallet is locked behind someone else’s key and rerouted toward an unknown loading dock. In this final step inside the logistics warehouse, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the high-bay pallet racks & forklift until the warehouse barcode inventory log catches the mismatch. Immediately upon AddMonitorW or on every subsequent OS boot, C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe (running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM) loads C:\Windows\System32\evilmon.dll (Sysmon EventID 7 ImageLoaded) and invokes InitializePrintMonitor2, spawning a SYSTEM child process under spoolsv.exe (logged in Sysmon Event 7 with EventID=7 , Sysmon ImageLoaded / 1 , Sysmon ProcessCreate, HostProcess=C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe , NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, UnsignedModule=C:\Windows\System32\evilmon.dll, ExportEntryPoint=InitializePrintMonitor2 so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes Sysmon EventID 7 (ImageLoaded): Image=C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe ImageLoaded=C:\Windows\System32\evilmon.dll Signed=false (which invokes or targets the host daemon/process , Sysmon EventID 7 , ImageLoaded: Image=C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe ImageLoaded=C:\Windows\System32\ so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1547.012 during "SYSTEM DLL Load in spoolsv.exe , Sysmon EventID 7 & Child Shell Execution , Sysmon EventID 1" , Immediately upon AddMonitorW or on every subsequent OS boot, C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact Sysmon EventID 1 (ProcessCreate): ParentImage=C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe -> Image=C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM) runs (which invokes or targets the host daemon/process , Sysmon EventID 1 , ProcessCreate: ParentImage=C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe -> Image=C:\Windows\Syst so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1547.012 during "SYSTEM DLL Load in spoolsv.exe , Sysmon EventID 7 & Child Shell Execution , Sysmon EventID 1" , Immediately upon AddMonitorW or on every subsequent OS boot, C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe loading unsigned evilmon.dll & spawning cmd.exe / ⇠#3 ACK 7) from Node ③ (#3 MS-RPRN \pipe\spoolss RPC) to Node ④ (#4 spoolsv.exe (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Print\Monitors & spool\PRINTERS).

keySpecs.value: Alert on any unsigned DLL loaded by spoolsv.exe (Sysmon EventID 7) and any interactive shell (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, rundll32.exe) with ParentImage=C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe.

steps.storyAnalogy: Lifting stacked pallets off the shelves, the driver slaps a brand-new shipping barcode and their own heavy padlock onto every customer crate in the bay. Here in Step 2 inside the logistics warehouse, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the logistics warehouse later without disturbing the quarantined audit cage.
steps.simpleExplanation: The attacker invokes winspool.drv!AddMonitorW (or RpcAddMonitor) to register evilmon.dll as a Print Port Monitor. This creates HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver="evilmon.dll" (Sysmon EventID 13) and logs Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational EventID 316 (Printer driver added) and EventID 808 (Failed/Untrusted plug-in module load in spoolsv.exe) (logged in WinEvent Event 808 with LogChannel=Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational, EventID=808 , Spooler Plug-in Load / 316 , Driver Added, RegistryPersistenceKey=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver, LoadedModule=C:\Windows\System32\evilmon.dll so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Under the hood, the observed step executes AddMonitorW(NULL, 2, &monitorInfo2) -> Registers Driver="evilmon.dll" (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , AddMonitorW, NULL, 2, &monitorInfo2 -> Registers Driver="evilmon.dll" via evilmon.dll, passi so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1547.012 during "Port Monitor Registration via AddMonitor & PrintService EventID 316 / 808" , The attacker invokes winspool while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact Registry Key: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver runs (which Modifies or queries Windows Registry keys and values , Registry Key: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver via th so that extracts the 16-byte SysKey / BootKey , stored across the JD, Skew1, GBG, and Data registry classes under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa required to decrypt the PEK and password hashes inside ntds.dit or SAM , T1547.012).

steps.detectionAndEvidence: Documented in WinEvent Event 808 (recording LogChannel=Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational, EventID=808 , Spooler Plug-in Load / 316 , Driver Added, RegistryPersistenceKey=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\EvilMonitor\Driver, LoadedModule=C:\Windows\System32\evilmon.dll under T1547.012): Enable the Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational event log (which is disabled by default on Windows) and alert on EventID 316, EventID 808, and Sysmon EventID 13 modifications under Control\Print\Monitors or Control\Print\Environments\*\Print Processors.
